subject: alebrije
pitch:
Category: Fantastical creature.
Subject: alebrije jaguar-eagle.
Style: Oaxacan alebrije painted wood.
reasoning:
I'm planning a single TypeScript module to render an alebrije-style jaguar-eagle hybrid, aiming for something richly detailed in the Oaxacan painted wood aesthetic while keeping the API usage correct since I can't test it. I'm sketching the creature's form: a jaguar's quadruped body combined with eagle wings and possibly an eagle head.

I'm thinking through proportions and anatomy — jaguar body and legs scaled chunky-alebrije style, a feathered crest, spread eagle wings around 2.2m across, and a tail fanning into feathers — along with the vibrant painted patterns like dots, zigzags, florals, and rosette spots I'll need as SVG textures layered onto the wood-carved look.

I'm planning the decal set: a concentric-ring alebrije eye, a dahlia flower motif, a sun/spiral forehead emblem, and painted feather cards in two colorways for the crest and cheek ruff. For the body paint, I'm working out custom cell-based rosette patterns in turquoise and black over a magenta/orange base, banded leg stripes, and feather-plate textures with stripes and dots extruded along the wings.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton for the jaguar head and body — placing the hips root, building a catmull spine curve from rump through hips, mid-body, chest, to neck base, and setting up a forward chain of spine joints parented to the hips.

I'll settle on count 3 with 3 names, giving three joints with no extra tip, and worry about whether the first spine joint coinciding with the hips position creates a zero-length bone—maybe I should offset the spine path's starting point slightly so it isn't identical to the hips joint.

Actually I recall the documented pattern treats the core as a shared root with chains radiating outward, so coincident joints at the root are expected and fine. For the tail, a jaguar-style curling tail ending in a feather fan can be its own chain or sprout off the hips, separate from the main body curve.

Decided to loft the body over the spine chain and give the tail its own independent sweep from the rump, using catmull-interpolated stations along z (rump, hips, mid, chest, front) with varying widths and heights.

Separating body loft and tail sweep will be easier to control than a single radius function across the whole curve. I'm nailing down actual coordinates now—hip and chest positions, body half-height, belly bottom, and leg joint placements for hips, shoulders, and feet.

For the legs I'm using a three-segment IK chain for the hind limbs (thigh, shin, metatarsal) to get a digitigrade stance, with the knee bending forward and the hock bending back, checking that the total segment length can reach the target distance from hip to ground. I'm setting up the joint chain naming and planning the paw shape at the tip.

For the foot I'm adding a flattened sphere as the main paw pad sitting right at ground level, plus four small toe spheres in front. For the front legs I'm using a two-segment shoulder-elbow-wrist chain with the elbow bending backward, adjusting the segment lengths so the reach matches the shoulder-to-ground distance, and now thinking through what the front foot/talon shape should look like for this jaguar-eagle hybrid creature.

I'm deciding to make the front feet eagle talons — yellow scaly skin with black claws, three forward toes and one back toe, each a tapered claw shape — while keeping the hind paws jaguar-style for a striking mix. To keep the joint count manageable I'll attach the talon toes as rigid parts directly on the wrist bone rather than giving each digit its own joint chain, though I'm considering adding a single joint per toe if it stays simple enough.

Now I'm planning the neck and head: a short two-joint neck chain rising from the chest into the head joint, sized to blend into the body, followed by a rounded jaguar-style skull with a projecting muzzle built from scaled spheres and boxes.

I'm figuring out the facial features — eye decals, rounded inner-colored jaguar ears, an eagle-style feather crest on top, and feathered cheek ruffs around the sides of the face. For the jaw, I'm placing a separate jaw joint with a lower jaw shape and upward teeth spikes, plus an upper muzzle built from a rounded shape with downward fangs.

I'm giving the mouth a slight open rest pose with a jaw joint that can tilt open around 12° to reveal a pink tongue and teeth, adding a dark triangular nose at the top-front of the muzzle, and now I'm working out the eagle wing structure as a three-segment chain (humerus, forearm, hand) spreading outward and slightly upward from the shoulders, defined with curve control points going from the chest area out to the wingtips.

Writing wing geometry...

Feathers extrude using the chain frame at a parameter along the bone. For painting, I'm defining a per-feather paint function based on normalized coordinates along length and width, allowing stripes, dots, and edge coloring, with many paint objects created for different feather sizes sharing the same sheet. Now I'm tallying feather counts per wing — primaries, secondaries, and so on.

I'm planning to add an underlying membrane plate beneath the wing feathers to avoid visible gaps, using the wing chain as one edge and an offset trailing path as the other edge, painted to blend with the feather colors on top.

Primary feathers near the hand fan outward toward the tip direction, and for the extrusion axes I'm computing the perpendicular tangent myself via Gram-Schmidt rather than relying on automatic orthogonalization, since the outline is symmetric so the exact sign of that axis doesn't matter.

Each wing bone root sits slightly below the arm, with coverts offset upward and shorter than secondaries, and layers spaced vertically by about 0.02 to prevent z-fighting given the 0.018 thickness. I'm working out the thickness axis via cross product for the left wing case, confirming the resulting normal direction doesn't matter since both faces are flat and painting depends only on the side parameter.

I'll build everything in its final rest pose first, then apply posing afterward since blend-skinned meshes get re-deformed — opening the jaw by about 14 degrees along its forward axis at the end. For the tail, I'm laying out a five-point curved chain from the rump using a Catmull-Rom path that curls upward, naming the segments tail1 through tail5.

Now for the tail tip, I want a fan of seven extruded feathers radiating outward with a taper from 0.08 to 0.035 and banded ring painting. I'm debating the orientation — a horizontal eagle-style fan wouldn't read well from the side, so I'm leaning toward a vertical crest-like fan in a tilted plane so it's visible from a side view while still having some depth.

This should create a vertical fan facing front/back, like a dramatic backdrop behind the head — a classic alebrije look. I'm mapping out the tail's curve from the rump upward and forward to establish the tip's tangent direction, which will anchor where the feather fan spreads from.

Now I'm checking the overall proportions — paw bottoms resting at floor level, claw tips spiking slightly above, and confirming the fan sits behind the body without clipping the head's height. Then I move to defining the head joint position and starting on the skull geometry using scaled spheres positioned relative to that joint.

Continuing with the muzzle, nose pad, fangs, and jaw joint placements as sphere and spike primitives offset from the head joint, with color choices like dark/pink for the nose pad.

Still working out jaw and skull orientation frames...

I need to be careful about the handedness here since model-local +x is world -X, so I'm switching to explicit "left/forward/up" naming in head.local calls to avoid sign confusion when mirroring the eye decal for each side.

Now I'm positioning the eye decal on the skull's ellipsoid surface, computing the forward offset so it sits flush against the curved sphere without overlapping the muzzle geometry, which sits lower and won't interfere at this height.

Recomputing the eye position with the adjusted muzzle geometry, I settle on slightly larger, more readable eyes rather than fiddling further with ring rims or brow ridges — simplest is to build them as subtly protruding domes placed directly at the eye coordinates.

Now I'm working out jaguar ears: round flattened discs with a smaller pink/turquoise inner disc set slightly forward, extruded with light smoothing and thickness, positioned relative to the head using local offsets scaled by model width.

Positioning the inner ear with a small forward offset so it reads centered on the drawing, then sketching the ear outline as a rounded shape built from points across and up from the root, smoothed slightly. Now I'm planning the crest: a row of 5-7 extruded feathers along the back of the skull, rising upward and backward, oriented so they read correctly from both side and front views.

Rethinking the crest layout — instead of feathers lying flat in a plane that'd look edge-on from the front, I want them fanning outward in an arc like an Aztec penacho headdress, spreading across from -55° to 55°, angled up and back, each rooted near the back of the head with a slight outward offset and varying length, with the feather's cross-section oriented using the world X axis so the planes face forward.

For rendering style, I'm deciding to use extruded painted bands (for a wood-carved look) on the crest, wings, and tail, while using textured double-sided card feathers for a neck ruff collar — a ring of angled feather cards standing outward around the neck joint, mimicking a jaguar-eagle mane.

I'm skipping fur details on paws and planning body decals instead: flower and sun/heart emblems painted on the shoulders and haunches, with rosette patterns, over a magenta-pink alebrije-style base color.

Writing paint shader code...

For the dotted ring I'll build a tangent basis from the normal to get an angular coordinate, then place dots where that angle falls into periodic bands within a radius range—cheap and effective. I'm also considering layering a fine dot grid across the base surface to mimic the dense puntillismo style common in alebrije patterns.

Now I'm defining paint logic for the belly with cream and turquoise chevrons, a magenta spine stripe edged in yellow using a zigzag function along the body axis, and banded leg patterns that alternate turquoise and magenta stripes with dot rows near the feet, falling back to body paint elsewhere.

For the wing membrane I'm using scallop bands across simple turquoise coloring, and for feathers I'm defining root, mid, and tip color zones along a normalized length coordinate, with a dark shaft line down the center, periodic dots, darker edge outlines, and an eye-spot marking near the tip.

Now I'm setting up a shading helper to warm highlights on top-facing normals and cool the underside, then defining the bright alebrije color palette—magenta, turquoise, cobalt, orange, yellow, lime, red, purple, cream, ink, and white.

For textures, I'm planning a decorative eye design with layered iris colors and turquoise dot accents, a magenta flower decal for haunches and shoulders, a sun spiral emblem for the forehead, two feather-pattern colorways for the neck ruff, and considering a heart motif placed low on the chest since the upper chest is mostly hidden by the ruff.

I'll skip claws, tongue, and wing membrane decals since they're not very visible, but I'm thinking about adding a small swirl texture inside the ears using a simple circular geometry.

So my final texture set lands at seven: eye, flower, sun, heart, swirl, and two ruff variants. I'll skip glow effects since this is painted wood, not something that should emit light, then move on to setting up the builder configuration with the piece name and paint size.

Checking texel density for a roughly 5m² painted surface at 2048 resolution gives about 1.3mm precision, which is plenty for fine 1cm dot details. Now I'm setting up the joint hierarchy, starting with the hips as root and building a spine chain through catmull-rom control points up to the chest, then moving into defining the body loft stations.

I'm working through the rump/spine joint ownership issue — worried about joints projecting past the bone's endpoints causing degenerate loft caps, so I'm repositioning the hips joint to sit at the rump and routing the spine curve forward through the chest toward the shoulders.

Loft stations before the first joint and past the last joint should default to belonging to the nearest joint, so the width/height interpolation and rounded caps should still work correctly end-to-end. Now I'm setting up the tail as a chain of five joints parented to the hips, with a sweep function defining its taper along the curve.

Next I'm placing a rigid feather fan at the tail's tip, anchoring it to the last tail joint's bone, then starting the neck as a three-point catmull chain parented off the spine.

Then I define the head joint sitting right at the neck's end, and attach a jaw joint positioned slightly forward and down from the head, aimed further out along the same direction.

I'm using word-based offsets like forward/up/down relative to the head's local frame for positioning, keeping orientation tied to that same frame via moved(). For the skull shape, I scale a sphere geometry asymmetrically so its width sits along local right, its length along the bone direction (forward), and height along up—since the sphere is symmetric, the pole orientation along that axis doesn't cause visual issues.

Rotating geometry to shift its poles...

Now I'm working out muzzle and nose placement: scaled sphere shapes positioned relative to the head joint, accounting for the ellipsoid curvature so the nose sits slightly forward and below the muzzle's peak.

I'm adding a nose bridge detail using a capsule stretching from between the eyes down to the nose in a contrasting paint color, plus small spherical whisker dots on each side of the muzzle before moving on to the whiskers themselves.

Working out the whisker placement, I'm adding three thin wire-like spikes per side angled outward from the muzzle, and now computing the fang geometry—using the muzzle's taper to figure out the base height, then placing downward spikes near the mouth for the upper fangs with a slight outward curve.

Now I'm setting up the lower jaw, figuring out its joint position and bone direction relative to the head frame, then sizing and positioning the jaw piece so its front edge sits slightly behind the muzzle tip.

Positioning the lower teeth as small spikes projecting upward from the jaw's local frame, then starting work on the tongue shape.

Now adding the mouth interior color, posing the jaw at a slight open angle, and placing the ears relative to the head with rounded outlines, bevels, and a magenta inner-ear detail plus a swirl texture layer.

Still positioning facial features...

I should also add a raised rim around each eye—a closed circle draped onto the skull surface, swept with a small yellow radius for a 3D highlight detail, built from a perpendicular basis around the eye center. Then for the crest, I'm planning 7 feathers rooted behind the skull top, spreading sideways, built as rigid extrusions.

Now I'm adding a cheek ruff of short feathers framing the face on both sides, angled outward from down to up, plus a neck ruff. For the wings, I'm adding a shoulder knob sphere, sweeping the wing arm along its leading edge, and building the membrane surface from the trailing edge points with some thickness.

Defining wing chain points...

Defining more feather rows...

Since both feather planes lie roughly in the same wing plane regardless of direction, the real fix is vertical stagger by alternating index, plus a slight downward droop for depth. I'll go with shingle-style overlapping rather than roll, and now I'm sketching out a feather paint function that maps root-mid-tip-edge-dot colors along each feather's length.

Instead of trying to compute the edge outline precisely, I'll approximate chevron bands using a combined u/v coordinate, cycling the color scheme across bands, with the shaft rendered in cream and dots placed at band centers.

For shading, I want the top and bottom faces of each feather to differ in warmth—top faces catching warm light, undersides falling into cool shadow—so I'm writing a lighting function that blends a warm and cool tone based on surface normal direction.

I'm also thinking the painted copal wood surface could use a subtle grain variation, multiplying color slightly by noise to suggest hand-painted texture.

For the tail, I'm designing banded rings alternating magenta, yellow, and turquoise with zigzag-edged borders and dot accents placed within the yellow bands, driven by the position along the tail and angle around it. I'm applying similar banded sock-like patterns to the legs based on vertical position.

For the hind paws, I'm shaping jaguar-style flattened paws with four toe beans, painting them magenta with dots and adding small exaggerated white claws for the alebrije style, keeping toes above ground level. For the front talons, I'm building an eagle-style foot starting with a scaled palm sphere at the base.

Still working out the toe and claw geometry...

I'm defining leg thickness with tapered radius arrays along the thigh-to-foot chain, checking that the hip joint's thigh radius still fits within the body's silhouette at that height.

Now I'm setting up the IK for hind and front legs, picking hip/shoulder positions, target foot positions, segment lengths, and bend directions, then verifying the shoulder-to-target distance stays just under the limb's total length so the leg reads as slightly bent rather than fully extended.

I'm defining the chain structure for each leg, mapping the IK joint points to named joints (shoulder/elbow/wrist for front, hip/knee/hock/foot for hind), parenting them to the spine, and setting up floor contact points for each foot.

For the neck ruff, I'm placing a ring of points around the neck at roughly a third of the way along its length, sized just inside the neck's taper radius, then generating card geometry (the ruff fur tufts) oriented with lean and bend parameters and some randomized variation.

I'll set the ring's tilt to zero and let the lean parameter control the mane-collar direction instead, then grab the items array from the ring's returned object for the card placement. For body decals, I'm adding flower decals near the haunches and hind thighs, positioning them by offsetting from the hip location.

Now I'm placing the HEART decal on the chest front and checking the loft dimensions so it lands cleanly below the chest bulge without the front legs intercepting the projection. Then I'm positioning a SUN decal on the forehead, aligning it with the skull's crest geometry.

Checking for overlap between the sun decal and the eye decals, I adjust the sun's size down to 0.085 and nudge it up to avoid z-fighting with nearby surface features, settling on a position atop the skull with the dir vector angled forward.

For the body I'm adding a row of cone-shaped spikes along the dorsal ridge, placing them at intervals along the spine between t 0.15 and 0.8 in alternating colors, each spike growing outward from its base along the surface normal to avoid floating off the mesh.

I'm considering adding a decorative beaded collar near the neck base, but worry it'd be buried inside the body loft since that section of the neck tube sits inside the torso geometry. Maybe better to place the collar higher up, around neck.at(0.55) or above the ruff cards, using a loop oriented along the neck's tangent frame so it's actually visible.

For the beads themselves, I need alternating colors, but the along-path callback only passes the point, not an index, so I'll just track a counter variable externally. The head-neck junction, chest underside, and feet all seem fine without extra detail.

For the tail fan, I'm placing 7 feathers of varying length at the tail's endpoint, oriented using the tangent and X directions, with bones attached to the last tail joint, plus a small wooden bead cuff ring at the base. With 5 tail joints and the last one positioned near the tip, I need to make sure the fan's bone references resolve correctly to that final joint, and the crest feathers should bind to the head bone.

Now I'm sketching out the eye SVG — concentric circles building up dark outer ring, golden base, a dotted pink ring, sclera, and a teal iris, layering shapes to create the eye's depth.

Now moving to the flower shape, I'm building eight rotated petals around a center point with magenta fill and ink outlines, then layering smaller yellow inner petals and a turquoise dotted center on top.

Next I'm sketching a sun with alternating orange and red triangular rays around a yellow disc, plus an inner red spiral and a ring of dots, before moving on to a sacred-heart design with a red heart shape and ink outline.

Still writing spiral code...

Now I'm sketching feather-shaped cards for the ruff design, with a curved tapering outline from base to tip and chevron band patterns layered on top.

I'm clipping the band and chevron details to the feather outline, adding a central shaft and dot accents, and setting up two colorways -- one in magenta/yellow/turquoise, another in cobalt/orange/lime. Writing shading function code...

Writing the body paint logic...

Then adding dorsal stripe coloring, rosette patterns, and speckle dots with a base orange-yellow noise gradient — though I realize the dorsal stripe condition might also incorrectly trigger on legs and head since they share the same y-axis check.

Writing rosette function...

I'm thinking through how the rosette size varies with feature point distance from the surface, giving smaller patterns farther away, and planning to restrict them to certain cell IDs for variety. Now I'm sketching the head paint logic—a yellow base with dot patterns around the muzzle and forehead regions.

Still writing paint logic...

Still defining paints for tail bands, wing arm stripes with zigzag dots, and membrane scallop rows across the wing skin.

Now I'm setting up ear, paw, and feather colorations, plus a reusable feather paint generator that colors the shaft, tip, and bands based on position along the length and width.

I need to remember TypeScript's unused parameter rules for the lit function signature, prefixing unused params with underscores and avoiding unused imports to pass typecheck. Now I'm defining the feather outline shape as a series of points sweeping from the base width out to a sharp tip and back.

I'm also considering the type for the outline array -- whether a plain tuple array can substitute for the SDK's OutlinePoint type, since importing that type directly from the builder module feels risky given the module boundaries.

Now I'm sketching a helper function to build feathers, computing orthonormal basis vectors from direction and side inputs, then calling the extrude function with position, orientation axes, and thickness parameters to generate each feather shape.

I'm checking the typing details — making sure the bone parameter accepts a Joint reference properly and that Vector3 inputs work directly as position/direction arguments without extra conversion, since these helper functions are defined as closures inside the main build function.

I'm naming the four wing points as wing1 through wingTip for each side, using a side label derived from whether s is positive or negative, and parenting them to the chest joint with a "wing" role. Then I'm thinking through how the wing chain's arc-length parameter t spans the whole path including the tip.

For the membrane, I build it between the leading edge chain and trailing points using the membrane helper with a thin wing-skin material, confirming tubes and membranes bend naturally with their span joints. I'm also checking that feather roots along the chain extend back past the membrane's leading-to-trailing slope, so their mostly horizontal planes sit correctly relative to the sloped membrane surface.

Checking for z-fighting between the membrane and feathers, I shorten the membrane's trailing edge so it only sits under the coverts, and work out offsets so coverts sit above the centerline while secondaries and primaries sit slightly below, keeping the membrane plane clear of the sloped feather geometry.

Instead of fighting coplanar overlaps, I decide to drop the membrane entirely and let overlapping feathers plus coverts do the job, then handle inter-feather z-fighting by giving each feather a slight shingle roll — rotating it a few degrees so adjacent feathers intersect along a clean line rather than lying flat against each other, combined with staggered offsets to avoid flicker.

I'll apply roughly 10° roll plus layer offsets per row (coverts raised, secondaries and primaries flush), computing the roll via the cross product of the feather's direction and up vectors. Counting feathers out: roughly 25 per wing across coverts, primaries, and secondaries, doubled for both wings, and I'm now considering adding a small ornamental sphere at the wrist joint and a row of stud-like dots along the arm.

Now I'm working out the front leg talons: placing a palm sphere at the wrist joint, then generating toes at forward angles of -30°, 0°, and 30° plus a back toe, each extending from the palm center outward.

That's close enough to the floor, so I'll leave it. I'm now considering whether to add a decorative cuff ring around the front ankle area, placing it along the leg sweep near the wrist using a loop surface oriented to the tangent frame.

Now I'm placing the hind paw spheres and toe clusters, positioning each toe with small offsets so they sit correctly against the ground plane.

I'm also adding tiny claw cones angled down and forward from each toe, checking the tip height stays just above zero. The hind foot joint doesn't need extra articulation since it's rigid at the tip, and I'm confirming scaling on the paw parts applies along world axes since no custom orientation is defined for them.

Now I'm working out the leg sweep radii — tapering values along the chain for both hind and front legs — and checking the front leg's top radius against the shoulder position to make sure it doesn't poke past the body's half-width.

Then I'm checking the wing root placement against the leg shoulder, and working through the neck-to-head connection: sizing the neck sweep so it's mostly buried under the chest loft and skull/ruff, keeping proportions compact and cute with an oversized alebrije-style head relative to body width, and double-checking the head isn't positioned too close to or overlapping the wing span.

Confirming the head sits forward of the wing roots in silhouette, then plotting the crest feathers extending up and back from the skull, checking their tips against the tail fan and wing tip heights for a clean overall silhouette, and now sketching out the tail curl points and fan feather radiation to shape the tail's upward sweep.

Working out the fan feather geometry so adjacent feathers don't overlap flatly in the same plane—applying a slight rolling rotation to each one, alternating the tilt so they shingle naturally like real tail feathers.

For coloring I'm assigning distinct gradient band schemes per feather group: secondaries get turquoise-cobalt-lime with magenta tips, primaries get magenta-purple-orange with cobalt tips, coverts get yellow-orange-red with turquoise tips, and the crest alternates between two palettes for visual variety.

I'm now setting up the cheek ruff feathers, defining per-side placement with root positions offset outward and back from the head, spreading angles symmetrically to create a fan shape, with shorter length and width than the main plumage.

I'm checking whether the crest feathers might collide with the ears and adjusting placement — moving the crest further back and up with more backward lean so its spread stays clear of the ears, which face forward.

Now I'm setting ear thickness and outline dimensions, then adding whiskers as thin colored rods extending from the muzzle sides with slight downward spacing per strand, plus small spheres placed on the muzzle surface to mark whisker dots. I'm starting to lay out the brows using a draped path.

For eyebrows, I draw a catmull curve through a few points and drape it onto the skull surface, then sweep a thin colored tube along it bound to the head bone. For eye rims, I create closed circular paths around each eye, drape them onto the skull, and sweep them into thin colored rings without end caps. I'm working out how to find the eye center on the surface by casting a ray inward from outside the head toward the eye direction to get a surface hit point for later decal placement.

For the eye rim, I'm building a circle basis perpendicular to the eye direction and sampling points along it, pulling them slightly forward before draping back to the skull surface. Then I'm placing the eye decal using the computed origin and direction, mirroring it for the opposite side, and considering whether both eyes should share the same highlight orientation for a more natural lit look.

Now I'm adding facial details: a small purple nose with a tiny white highlight sphere, a pink tongue, and a dark flattened sphere for the inner upper palate placed under the muzzle, visible when the jaw opens. I'm also planning spine spikes distributed along the body using an alternating color pattern.

Still placing dorsal spikes...

For flower decals, I can target the body loft directly since decal targets accept any surface the sweep produces. I'm checking whether a neck collar would be visible between the ruff and head—tracing the neck path's position at various points against the skull's bounding sphere to see if it gets occluded.

Rather than add a collar, I'll just lengthen the neck slightly for readability, adjusting the path points from the base up to the head joint, and shifting the skull center forward and up accordingly. The neck ends up barely visible in a narrow band, which is acceptable, with the ruff positioned earlier along that path.

Checking overall proportions now — total height with the fan comes to about 1.75, and the head-to-front-leg spacing works out fine with the muzzle sitting forward of the front feet. I'm setting a mild jaw-open angle and defining the jaw as its own rig component, then building the ruff using textured cards with randomized lean, bend, and spin variation for a natural look.

I'm placing a ring around the neck at the 0.4 point, computing the interpolated neck radius there so the ring sits just inside the surface with the cards rooted and sinking slightly in. I'm working through how each card's orientation flattens against the outward-facing plane depending on whether it's on the top or bottom of the neck, so the flow direction naturally leans back along the curve either way.

Now I'm checking how the heart decal on the chest sits relative to the ruff cards above it—since the bottom-front ruff cards lean down and back, they'll partially cover the top of the chest, so I'm working out the front surface z-position at that height and sizing the heart decal's x-extent against the leg positions so it fits cleanly between them.

Next I'm placing a sun emblem on the flanks at mid-body, checking the body's half-width there against the wings and leg positions to confirm the mid-flank area stays clear for it. Then I'm adding a flower decal near the haunch with its own size and direction, and considering whether rosette paint on the skull cheeks would work too, before moving on to planning cuff loops around the leg sweeps at specific points along the front and hind leg chains.

Now I'm working out the sweep loop radius and spacing eight alternating-colored beads along the loop path, using a bead placement function that follows the path's frame so each bead inherits position and bone influence. I'm noting that the loop itself should carry blended skin weights along its length, then considering whether to skip adding a carved joint bead at the knee or elbow, and starting to think through a ring of small feather cards around the front leg's upper section for a feathered-pants look.

Adding ruff texture cards with downward flow for that eagle-like touch, then tallying up the joint count across hips, spine, tail, neck, head, wings, legs and toes to confirm it totals 43. I'm also sketching a rough tally of part counts — body loft, spikes, decals, head details, crest, cheek feathers, ears, eye rims, brows, whiskers, dots, and wings — to get a sense of overall model complexity.

Now I'm estimating the full parts total across arms, studs, feathers, shoulder knobs, legs, paws, talons, cuffs, beads, tail fan, and cards, landing around 250 parts. Then I'm roughly calculating triangle counts from feather extrusions and bevels to make sure the total polygon budget stays under 60k.

Studs are simple low-poly spheres, so those are cheap. Now I'm setting up the imports for the builder SDK, pulling in geometry and color utilities like catmull, bezier, noise, mix, and paint types, and checking whether `limb` is properly re-exported from the package's main index.

I'm defining the module metadata export with the alebrije's name and description, then building a `lit` helper that wraps a shading function to resolve colors against surface position and normal using the paint system, making sure the surface coordinate types line up correctly.

Writing color palette constants...

Still defining rosette ring logic...

I'm also weighing the performance cost: this paint function runs per texel across a body area of roughly 2 m² at ~766 texels/m, so around 1.2 million texels, each potentially calling the cell-stripe logic multiple times—heavy but should stay within JS's throughput.

Doing the math more precisely, that could add up to billions of operations, which risks multi-second render times, so I'm considering dropping the paint canvas resolution to 1024 instead of 2048 to cut texel count roughly in half and keep things responsive, accepting a coarser ~2.6mm texel density as a tradeoff.

Writing body color logic...

Still writing leg sock pattern logic...

For paws I'll use a yellow ring pattern over magenta base, and for the head I'm layering a rosette pattern with cobalt/red dot cells and a yellow-orange gradient blend based on normal direction and noise, with the muzzle kept a simple cream color.

Now I'm defining the muzzle pattern with turquoise spaced dots over cream, and setting the jaw to cream with a red stripe using the muzzle paint for the lower section. For the tail, I'm setting up a color sequence array and building a segment-based index calculation to cycle through those colors along the tail's length.

Still writing wing arm colors...

Negative k edge cases seem fine for the modulo logic. Now I'm moving on to the actual builder function, starting with setting up the paint canvas size for the jaguar-eagle alebrije.

Building the skeleton joints...

Still defining the tail joint chain...

I'm double-checking the naming convention for tail joints and confirming the neck catmull spline produces the right number of segments without an extra tip joint. For the jaw and head, I'm using model-relative directions so pitch doesn't skew the forward/down offsets, while frame-oriented geometry still follows the head's own axes. Now I'm starting the loop to build the left and right leg chains symmetrically.

Adding paw sphere geometry...

Now setting up the front leg chain, defining shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints with a parent at the chest.
